Michelangelo's David stands in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence at night, marble luminous under museum spotlights, the domed skylight above, empty galleries around him, the sling over his shoulder, his gaze turned aside. The camera drifts slowly up from the base of his plinth, an ordinary quiet night in the museum.

Then a seam of light cracks through the marble and races across his body, and his eyes ignite. Stone grinds against stone as he turns his head, marble dust cascading from his shoulders in sheets. He steps down off the plinth, the floor cratering under his weight, a shockwave rolling outward that shatters the skylight above into a cascade of falling glass. He straightens to his full colossal height, moonlight pouring down through the broken dome onto white marble.

He reaches back for the sling on his shoulder and swings it once, twice, faster, the stone whistling in a widening arc, marble muscles flexing and cracking with the motion — then he HURLS it. The release detonates, a ring of force exploding outward, glass and dust blasting past the camera, columns splitting.

THE ACTION MOVES CONTINUOUSLY FORWARD AND NEVER RESETS — the statue never returns to its original pose. He follows through into the throw, body pitched forward, and throws his head back and ROARS, breath steaming, rain pouring through the shattered dome and running down white marble, lightning flashing through the broken roof behind him. THE FINAL FRAME holds mid-roar, head thrown back, arm still extended from the throw.

CAMERA: starts high and wide, then plunges down along his body as he steps off, whips around him low at ground level as he draws the sling, snaps back on the release, and finally cranes up his chest to his face as he roars against the lightning.

Epic blockbuster cinematography, colossal scale, volumetric light through falling dust and glass, rain, anamorphic lens flares, film grain. Sound of grinding stone, shattering glass, the whistle of the sling, a deafening roar, thunder.

The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island under a blazing hot sun, harsh midday light, no clouds, tourists and boats tiny in the harbor far below, Manhattan skyline behind her. She has been holding the torch up for over a century and she is DONE.

Her expression shifts from stoic to visibly irritated — brow furrowing, a slow exasperated exhale, her free arm dropping to rest on her hip. She lowers the torch and rolls her shoulder like it's stiff. Close-up on her face: unmistakable annoyance, the look of someone who has had enough.

She tosses the torch — it arcs and falls, hitting the harbor water and sending up a column of spray, still burning on the surface. She steps up onto the edge of her pedestal, crown catching the light, and looks down at the water with the look of someone about to finally get some relief.

She DIVES. The colossal copper body arcs through the air and plunges into the harbor, an enormous splash exploding outward, water surging over nearby boats. THE FINAL FRAME holds on the water settling, only her crown and part of her face breaking the surface, eyes closed, a look of pure relief.

CAMERA: starts wide on her stoic pose, pushes into the face for the irritation beat, pulls back and low as she tosses the torch, tracks alongside her dive, then settles on the floating crown.

Comedic but still cinematic, warm bright sunlight, playful golden-hour color near the end, film grain. Sound of a tired exhale, a splash, harbor ambience, seagulls.

A row of colossal Moai statues stands on the windswept grass slope of Easter Island at dusk, backs to the ocean, volcanic stone weathered and lichen-stained, the Pacific crashing on black rock below, storm clouds massing on the horizon. THE ACTION MOVES CONTINUOUSLY FORWARD AND NEVER RESETS — the statues never return to their original positions.

First, deep fissures of light crack through the volcanic rock of the nearest Moai and race along the whole row, and their heavy-lidded stone eyes ignite one by one down the line. Stone grinds against stone as the first Moai rocks forward, shedding centuries of soil and lichen in sheets, and TEARS free of the earth with a shuddering boom, the ground splitting and heaving around its base. It takes one enormous step forward, then another, each footfall cratering the turf and sending shockwaves rolling out through the grass. One by one the entire row wrenches free and begins to walk, an unstoppable procession of giants marching down the slope toward the sea, dust and earth streaming from their shoulders, the ground trembling with every synchronized step. They keep advancing, growing closer and larger, until the lead Moai fills the frame and its vast stone face tilts down toward the camera. THE FINAL FRAME holds on that face looking down, eyes burning, still mid-stride with one foot lifted, the others striding behind it — the procession is still marching as the shot ends.

CAMERA: starts low in the grass looking up along the row, whips down the line as the eyes ignite in sequence, cranes back and low as the first one tears free, tracks alongside the marching row at ground level with the earth shaking, then falls back and cranes up into the lead statue's face as it looms over the lens.

Epic blockbuster cinematography, colossal scale, volumetric storm light, dust and flying earth, wind-lashed grass, anamorphic lens flares, film grain. Sound of grinding stone, thunderous earth-shaking footfalls, howling wind, crashing surf, distant thunder.
